title: SALT: Frozen Teachers for Video Learning
one_liner: Use a frozen teacher instead of a constantly-updating one to learn video representations more efficiently and transparently.
lead: Video models need to understand what is happening in videos without being told the answer. The standard trick is to hide some patches (regions) and train the model to guess what is hidden using a teacher model that slowly updates itself. This paper shows you can freeze the teacher instead: train it once to predict pixels, then freeze it, and train the student to predict what the frozen teacher sees. This is simpler because the training loss tells you if the model is working, faster because teacher and student can now be scaled independently, and works better because there are no moving targets confusing the student's learning.

problem.h2: Why video models struggle to learn without labels
paras: A video model needs to learn what objects and actions look like without someone telling it the answers (the ground truth). The old way: hide some video patches and have a slowly-updating teacher tell the student what is hidden. The teacher is not frozen; it constantly learns too, which means the target keeps shifting.

This creates two problems. First, picking which model to save is hard: the training loss during learning does not tell you if the model will be good at the real task. Second, the teacher and student are tightly tangled together, so you cannot use a tiny teacher with a big student. This wastes compute.

callout.html: You train a teacher that keeps changing. The student chases a moving target. Picking the best model is guesswork. Training is wasteful.

steps.text: Train one encoder to predict raw pixel values of hidden video patches using simple reconstruction loss. Train it for N steps, then freeze it permanently.

Train a student encoder to predict what the frozen teacher sees (in feature space, not pixels), only on hidden patches. A mathematical stop-sign prevents update signals from flowing backward to the teacher.
The student's training loss is a real distance metric that correlates with downstream task accuracy. No complex momentum math. You know if it is working.
Teacher and student are fully separate. You can use a tiny teacher (40k steps) with a large student (80k steps) without any coupling penalty.

The frozen student becomes your video feature extractor. It works as well as the old momentum method because the two-stage design (pixel reconstruction then feature matching) achieves the same learning goals without the complexity; it is faster because teacher and student are no longer coupled, so you pay zero overhead for training the teacher; it is easier to understand because the loss is a real distance metric that tells you if learning is working.

paras: The teacher mechanism switches from exponential moving average (EMA) update — where the teacher slowly shifts at every training step — to a static freeze — the teacher is trained once and never changes again. This single change ripples through: loss becomes interpretable, model selection becomes reliable, and teacher-student coupling vanishes.

hidden.h2: The hidden quantity: Student loss correlation
hidden.name: Loss-to-accuracy correlation (R-squared)
paras: In the old EMA-based methods, the loss the model sees during training does not tell you whether the model will actually work well on the real task. It is noise. This paper discovers a hidden quantity: how strongly the student's training loss predicts downstream task accuracy. With a frozen teacher, this correlation becomes very strong (measured as R-squared, which is 0 when random, 1 when perfect).

The paper measures this by training many student models, recording their loss during training, then testing them on real video tasks and computing the correlation. With SALT, the R-squared is 0.984, meaning the training loss is almost a perfect signal of how good the model will be. This is huge: it means you can pick the best model just by watching the loss.

heat.caption: Darker means training loss predicts downstream accuracy better. Frozen teacher method (steps 4-8) shows strong signal.

reads.html: Watch the training loss. If it is dropping steadily, the model will be good at the real task. No guessing.

The student loss serves as an informative, training-time metric that correlates strongly with downstream accuracy under frozen-backbone evaluation, in contrast to EMA-based methods that require proxy heuristics for model selection.

mechanism.h2: Why freezing the teacher makes everything better
paras: When the teacher updates at every step (EMA), the student is always chasing a moving target. Imagine teaching someone to throw a ball at a hoop, but the hoop keeps sliding. Every correction the student makes might be wrong by next step because the hoop moved. The student's loss does not mean much; the model might be great but just unlucky this step.

When you freeze the teacher, the target becomes stable and honest. The student learns a real skill: predicting a fixed thing. The training loss now measures real progress. Because the student is no longer trying to match a constantly-shifting teacher, the loss is clean. You can look at it and know the model is learning well.

Second, the frozen teacher untangles teacher and student. In the old method, if you want a bigger student, you need a proportionally bigger teacher to keep up. They are coupled. With a frozen teacher, you train it once (even tiny) and then train students of any size on it. A small teacher handles the hard pixel-reconstruction task (a simple job). The large student focuses on learning distinctive patterns in video (the complex job). Each specializes. This is like hiring a small specialist to teach a large team: the small specialist does not get tired and does not scale with team size.

stages.s: Frozen teacher encodes frame to pixel-space predictions
Student encoder predicts what frozen teacher sees
Measure difference (this is the real loss signal)
Student learns stable features for video understanding

math.words: Student loss equals the average distance between student's prediction and frozen teacher's output on masked regions, with no gradient flowing back to the teacher.

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Teacher was trained to output [0.9, 0.1, 0.8] for a hidden patch.
Student predicts [0.8, 0.2, 0.9] for the same patch.
Frozen teacher: teacher stays [0.9, 0.1, 0.8] forever. Student learns to predict it exactly.
EMA teacher: teacher might drift to [0.88, 0.12, 0.79] on the next step. Student's loss suddenly changes even though it learned nothing new.

math.note: The frozen teacher is a stable ground truth. The student learns to match it. No moving targets.

charts.title: Old EMA-based method (V-JEPA 2)
charts.note: Teacher and student tied together. Training loss is not predictive. Harder to scale.

charts.title: SALT frozen-teacher method
charts.note: Teacher and student separate. Training loss predicts accuracy (R-squared 0.98). Tiny teacher scales to big student.

items.html: If Stage 1 trains the teacher poorly (e.g., wrong masking pattern, bad data, too few steps), the frozen teacher becomes a bad reference. The student can only learn to mimic a bad teacher.

items.b: Teacher trained for too few steps.
items.html: If the teacher barely trains (say, 5 steps), it has not learned much. The student will predict something useless. But this is easy to catch: the training loss will be huge and the model selection metric will scream. The paper shows that with enough teacher training (40+ steps), even modest teacher quality works.

items.b: Frozen teacher does not cover the space.
items.html: If the teacher only learned to predict patches of one video type, a student trained on different video types will see patches the teacher never modeled. Predictions will be garbage. Stay in the same domain.
Train the teacher thoroughly on pixel reconstruction (Stage 1). Monitor the training loss in Stage 2. Pick the student when the loss plateaus. The frozen teacher does the job.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a tiny video representation learning pipeline: download a small video dataset (e.g., Kinetics subset or home videos), implement the two-stage process (Stage 1 trains a teacher to reconstruct masked pixels, Stage 2 trains a student to predict the frozen teacher's features on masked patches), and show that the student's training loss tracks downstream accuracy on a small action-recognition task.
demo.closing: The demo should make it impossible to miss: as the training loss drops, the student's accuracy on real video tasks climbs in lockstep. The loss is honest. No moving goalposts.
